text: Are the stereotypes about women true? Part 2. I'm back and I'm not done yet. This lady just doesn't stop. She keeps debunking stereotypes about women. And who am I to say no to that? Number 1. Women are bad with money. Multiple studies show that women are more likely to have an emergency fund, more likely to stick to a budget, and more likely to seek out financial advice before making big decisions. Women also often get accused of spending emotionally, when in actuality we're just expected to make less money stretch further, on average earning 82 cents per dollar that a man makes. Goldman Sachs research found that that income gap alone could create a 24% shortfall in women's retirement savings. We're not bad with money. We're dealing with less of it and still outperforming. Okay, let's try to address the stereotype that women are bad with money. It seems like her claim, though, is that women are actually better than men with money. The truth is once again more nuanced. First, let's look at financial knowledge and literacy. Most large international studies, OECD, Federal Reserve, etc., find that men score slightly higher on financial literacy tests. Some do claim, though, that it is partly due to test behavior and confidence of men. Not necessarily knowledgeability. Second, day-to-day money management. Again, if you look at large surveys like OECD, Federal Reserve, FINRA, women on average do show more disciplined day-to-day financial behavior. They are more likely to budget, more likely to save, and less likely to take on risky debt. Third, investing behavior. This one is the most interesting part. It does seem like men tend to trade more frequently, take more risks, and be more overconfident, while women tend to trade less, be more patient, and make fewer impulsive decisions. For example, one of the most cited papers in behavioral finance, Boys Will Be Boys, by Barber and Odeon, found that men traded significantly more than women, which hurt their returns and led to underperformance compared to women. Now, does that mean that women are better investors overall? Not really. Partly because the investing behavior data is largely based on retail investors, regular people managing their own accounts. While most of the assets in financial markets are managed and invested institutionally, where men do have overrepresentation. But it does seem like overall there is a pattern that women tend to be more risk-averse, while men tend to be more risk-seeking. This leads to women on average making fewer big mistakes, but also missing opportunities, while men having higher upside potential, but also more losses. Overall, it is hard to say who is better with money, men or women. But it does seem like the stereotype that women are bad with money does not really hold up when you look at the data. Because if we say that women are bad with money, then based on the same logic, we would also have to say that men are bad with money too. Now quickly one thing regarding gender pay gap that she mentioned in her speech. I probably need to make a separate video on it, but generally speaking, this notion has already been debunked many times. Yet media and some women keep bringing it up over and over again. Guys, if you control for comparable factors, profession, age, education, hours worked, the gender pay gap becomes very small or disappears. And in some cases, it can even reverse, with women earning slightly more than men. But once again, this topic probably deserves its own video.
